agents.name: claude
agents.description: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed.

agents.name: Explore
agents.description: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions.

agents.name: general-purpose
agents.description: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you.

agents.name: Plan
agents.description: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs.

agents.name: statusline-setup
agents.description: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting.

content.text:
Canada is the second-largest country in the world by total area, at about 9.98 million square kilometres. It spans six time zones (seven counting Newfoundland's half-hour offset) and stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific to the Arctic Ocean. It has the longest coastline of any country, over 200,000 km, and shares the longest international land border in the world with the United States, roughly 8,900 km including the Alaska boundary.

## Geography and Climate

**Regions.** Canada is often divided into five broad regions:
- **The Atlantic provinces** (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador): rugged coastlines, fishing heritage, and the Bay of Fundy, which has the highest tides on Earth.
- **Central Canada** (Ontario and Quebec): the industrial and population heartland, centred on the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River.
- **The Prairies** (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta): vast agricultural plains, plus major oil and gas, potash, and uranium production.
- **The West Coast** (British Columbia): mountains, temperate rainforest, and the Pacific ports.
- **The North** (Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut): sparsely populated Arctic and subarctic land, with a large Indigenous share of the population.

**Landforms.** The Canadian Shield, an ancient Precambrian rock formation, covers nearly half the country and is rich in minerals, lakes, and boreal forest. The Rocky Mountains and Coast Mountains run along the west. Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined, and about 20% of the world's freshwater is found within its borders, though much of that is in glaciers and groundwater.

**Climate.** It varies enormously: mild, wet winters in Vancouver; harsh continental extremes on the Prairies; humid summers in southern Ontario; and polar conditions in the Arctic. Most Canadians live within about 150 km of the US border, since that is where the climate is most hospitable.

## People and Demographics

The population is roughly 40 to 41 million. It is heavily urbanized, with the largest metropolitan areas being Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Ottawa-Gatineau, Calgary, and Edmonton.

Immigration drives most population growth. Canada admits several hundred thousand permanent residents per year, and more than one in five residents was born abroad. Large communities trace their roots to South Asia, China, the Philippines, the Caribbean, the Middle East, and Europe. Policy around temporary residents and international students has been tightened in recent years in response to housing pressure.

**Languages.** English and French are the two official languages at the federal level. About three-quarters of the population speak English as a first language, and roughly 20-22% speak French, concentrated in Quebec, where French is the sole provincial official language. New Brunswick is officially bilingual. Indigenous languages such as Cree, Inuktitut, and Ojibwe are spoken by smaller numbers, and many are endangered.

## History

**Indigenous peoples.** First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples have lived on this land for at least 15,000 years, with diverse societies, trade networks, and governance systems. Indigenous peoples make up about 5% of the population today.

**European arrival.** Norse settlers briefly occupied L'Anse aux Meadows around 1000 CE. Jacques Cartier claimed land for France in 1534, and Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608. The fur trade shaped early relationships among France, Britain, and Indigenous nations. Britain won control of New France in the Seven Years' War, confirmed by the Treaty of Paris (1763). The Quebec Act of 1774 protected French civil law and Catholic religion.

**Confederation.** The British North America Act created the Dominion of Canada on July 1, 1867, with Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. Other provinces joined over time: Manitoba (1870), British Columbia (1871), PEI (1873), Alberta and Saskatchewan (1905), and Newfoundland (1949). Nunavut was created as a territory in 1999. The transcontinental Canadian Pacific Railway, completed in 1885, was central to national unity, and its construction relied on exploited Chinese labour.

**Growing autonomy.** Canada fought in both World Wars, with Vimy Ridge (1917) often cited as a moment of national identity. The Statute of Westminster (1931) gave legislative independence, and the Constitution Act of 1982 "patriated" the constitution and added the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Quebec's government did not sign it, and Quebec sovereignty referendums were held in 1980 and 1995, the latter failing by a margin of about 1%.

**Difficult history.** Residential schools forcibly separated Indigenous children from their families for over a century, the last closing in 1996. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2015) called it cultural genocide and issued 94 Calls to Action. Other injustices include the Chinese head tax, the internment of Japanese Canadians in WWII, and the turning away of the *Komagata Maru*.

## Government and Politics

Canada is a **federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy**. The monarch (King Charles III) is head of state, represented by the Governor General. The Prime Minister, usually the leader of the party with the most seats in the House of Commons, is head of government. The Senate is appointed, not elected. The House has 338 members elected by first-past-the-post.

Powers are divided between federal and provincial governments: provinces control health care, education, and natural resources, while Ottawa handles defence, criminal law, and trade, among others. The legal system is common law, except in Quebec, where private law follows the civil law tradition. The Supreme Court has nine justices.

The major federal parties are the Liberals, Conservatives, NDP, Bloc Québécois, and Greens. Mark Carney became Liberal leader and Prime Minister in March 2025 and won the April 2025 election.

## Economy

Canada has one of the world's ten or so largest economies, with a high standard of living. It is a member of the G7, G20, OECD, and NATO.

- **Resources:** oil (the oil sands in Alberta hold some of the world's largest reserves), natural gas, hydroelectricity, minerals, timber, and agriculture. Canada is a leading exporter of wheat, canola, and potash.
- **Manufacturing:** autos and aerospace, concentrated in Ontario and Quebec.
- **Services and finance:** Toronto is a major financial centre, and the banking system is dominated by a few large banks that fared well in the 2008 crisis.
- **Technology:** hubs in Toronto-Waterloo, Montreal, Vancouver, and Ottawa, with notable strength in AI research.

Trade is deeply tied to the US, which takes the large majority of exports. The USMCA (formerly NAFTA) governs North American trade, and tariff disputes with the US since 2025 have pushed Canada to diversify its trading partners.

## Society and Public Policy

- **Health care:** publicly funded, universal coverage for medically necessary hospital and physician services, administered by the provinces under the Canada Health Act. Wait times and physician shortages are persistent problems.
- **Social policy:** same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide in 2005, cannabis in 2018, and medical assistance in dying in 2016. Gun control is stricter than in the US.
- **Multiculturalism:** adopted as official policy in 1971 and enshrined in the Charter, it is central to the national self-image.
- **Housing affordability** is a major concern, especially in Toronto and Vancouver.

## Culture

- **Sport:** hockey is the national winter sport and lacrosse the national summer sport. Canada also loves curling, basketball (invented by Canadian James Naismith), and soccer, and co-hosted the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
- **Food:** poutine, butter tarts, Nanaimo bars, maple syrup (Canada produces most of the world's supply), Montreal bagels and smoked meat, and a wide range of immigrant cuisines.
- **Arts:** writers such as Margaret Atwood, Alice Munro, and Michael Ondaatje; the Group of Seven painters; musicians from Joni Mitchell and Leonard Cohen to Drake and The Weeknd; and Indigenous art traditions including Inuit carving and Haida work.
- **Symbols:** the maple leaf flag (1965), the beaver, the loon, and the RCMP. The national anthem is "O Canada."

## Foreign Policy and the World

Canada has long favoured multilateralism, a role in UN peacekeeping, and alliances through NATO and NORAD. It is a member of the Commonwealth and La Francophonie. Its relationship with the US is the most important and sometimes the most strained. Arctic sovereignty, climate change, and the opening of Arctic shipping routes are growing strategic issues.

## Challenges Ahead

Key issues include reconciliation with Indigenous peoples and unresolved land claims, balancing resource development with climate commitments, wildfires and warming that is occurring about twice as fast in the Arctic, housing and cost of living, health care capacity, and economic dependence on a single trading partner.

If you'd like, I can go deeper on any section, such as the history of Confederation, Indigenous rights, the provinces individually, or the economy.
